Al Gafa

Al Gafa has fashioned a career as a skilled guitar accompanist and soloist on stage and in the studio. Highlights in his career included extended stints with Carmen McRae and Dizzy Gillespie, and studio work with artists including Paul Simon and Kai Winding.
Al was interviewed via Zoom on May 2, 2023 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe and I’m very pleased to have Al Gafa with me today, a well known guitar player and I’d like to start out with a question: When you meet someone new and someone your age and invariably a question comes up well what did you do for your career? How do you answer that? Do you have a short answer for that?

I just tell them I’m a musician. That’s the first thing. And then of course they always ask well what instrument do you play and I tell them guitar, and we go from there. But it doesn’t always work that smoothly. I’ve got to tell you a story at the beginning of this thing, if you don’t mind. We invited a couple over to the house at one time and that same question came up, he said, “What do you do for a living?” And at that time I was playing the Broadway show “Annie.” So I said, “I’m a musician.” He said, “Oh, what instrument do you play?” I said, “Well in this show I’m playing guitar and banjo.” And he said, “Oh I love the banjo.” And I knew it was really going to be a long evening. Okay? So when I do answer that question I always tell them that I’m a musician and the following question is always well what instrument do you play, and it’s the guitar and that’s it. You know. And then if they want to take it further I take it further. I don’t really talk about my career too much for the sake of talking about my career.

It’s such a varied thing because musicians traditionally have worn so many hats in order to make a living that it is a hard thing to explain and when you say someone played the banjo they probably immediately get this impression of you playing in a Shakey’s Pizza or something you know, playing Dixieland.

Yeah, I didn’t mean to interrupt but you know here in the United States, well you go to Europe and you tell them you’re a musician they go, “Oh, you’re a musician.” But here in the United States you tell them you’re a musician and they say, “Well is that the way you make a living? Do you make enough money? Are you a waiter?” You know it’s all other things. So there’s a different concept of a musician in the United States and a musician in Europe.
Did your parents have this, like a bit of worry when they saw you heading towards a career as a musician? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

If they had a worry they never voiced it. You know my mom was born in America, my father was born in Europe, and there was never a decision to become a musician. I was able to play the guitar and I got a job and I’ve been working ever since. So it was never like I was going to devote my life to being a musician it just happened and I just stayed with it. And I know my father was extremely proud of my career, yeah.

That’s nice to hear. Yeah, I listened to an interview that you did with a fella named Jake and you had said that it was a hobby, it was fun. Did it become, like in high school, people, high school people, especially guys sort of get an identity you know, quarterback or they own hot cars or something. Did that become your identity as a guitar player?

No. In fact it was way in the background in high school. I studied engineering in high school and the guitar was the hobby for me. It was not something that I was really focused on. I did it and, oh I’ll tell you a story though, if you don’t mind all these little stories.
That’s why we’re here.

Okay. I played baseball for the high school team. And just when I made the team I started getting calls for recording sessions after school. And they would set up the recording sessions. Because I was in school they would wait for school to be out. So I had to quit the baseball team to go in the studio. And the coach kind of never forgave me and he said, “How could you quit baseball for music?” And that’s — it wasn’t too encouraging but I never looked back at it too much.

I love that. “We can’t start the session yet, Al’s on his way from high school.” You know this was on my list of topics because I’m fascinated by those recording sessions at the time. You had stated that in the early 60s money was being thrown around in the music business. Can you extrapolate on that a little bit?

Okay yeah. First of all my recording work started — I auditioned with a, it was a doo- wop group. They had an audition with two really well known artists, Doc Pomus and Morty Shuman. They wrote many Ray Charles hits and Andy Williams. They went to play an audition and they asked me to play the audition with them. And at the audition Morty Shuman, he was the keyboard player, he asked me if I would like to do recording sessions. So I’m just — it was a hobby of mine, yeah sure, okay, what’s a recording session? Let’s find out what it is. So I got started in the business like that. And when I graduated high school I went into the Navy and so I actually cut that recording session thing short because I went in the service. When I got out of the service I looked them up again and they threw me right back in and that’s how it started. Okay. Now I forgot the other part of your question.
Those first sessions, like that first audition, did they put music in front of you? Chord charts or what? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

At the audition it was a group auditioning for them when the music had been rehearsed and all, and so that part was done. But when we were in the studio it was mostly chord charts, yes. And I need to tell you about the — these were demos. The business at that time was that writers would write a song and then they would go in the studio and record it and make this demonstration record and then mail these demonstration records out to the various artists. We would go through the publishing company and mail it out. And the guys that I started working for was this Doc Pomus and Morty Shuman, and the rhythm section, you need to know about this because Panama Francis was the drummer, Morty played piano on most of the things, Leonard Gaskin was the bass player, another old time bass player a good bass player, Kenny Burrell was the other guitar player, King Curtis was the saxophone player. So — and oh the vocalist on most of these things was Bobby Darin. So now right, I would say within a month of these sessions starting Bobby Darin relocated to California because he had “Splish Splash” was a big hit and that was the last time we saw him except we’d see him in a movie or two but not back in the demo studios anymore. So that was the rhythm section and those things didn’t go through the union and every morning you’d go to the mailbox and there’d be another check for another date or something like that. It was quite lucrative at the time. And at that time you were in the studios to record these demos and everybody was throwing money into the demo field to possibly get a hit because when the hits hit they were big money, big money results from the hits.
Did the demos ever become the actual record?

No, but no. But a lot of times stuff that we did on the demos was just copied and taken to be in somebody’s arrangement, but it was really ours in the studio. You know we’d try stuff out in the studio and something would sound good or it wouldn’t sound good and we’d change it until everybody was happy and then we did it.
Did you ever find that aggravating? Like there’s this other group of musicians who are now basically copying what we did and they’re probably getting more money?
Well yeah. I think that was just part of the whole thing. You couldn’t stop it and we, if we had a stronger record than they did, we did. That was it. It was over.
How did you and Kenny Burrell decide — divide the guitar parts? I’ll do this, you do that, you do the — one person does the chics or whatever.
Yeah. I was the chic guy I think and Kenny was the rhythm guy, yeah. That’s a good way to describe it, yeah.
Did ego, I’ll rephrase, was ego allowed in these situations?

There were egos but not in the sense that your question is saying. You do this part because I can do it better, it was never anything like that. And if I was playing something the other musicians — I’m not saying Kenny wasn’t always on it, sometimes I was the © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

only guy on it. And if they liked what I played okay. If they didn’t like what I played try this, I’ll try this. So egos would only get in the way. There were a lot of guys that had different kinds of egos. Like the drummer for Aretha Franklin, Bernard Purdie —
Bernard Purdie.
I don’t know, do you know —
Yes.

So when we’d go into a studio Bernard Purdie would set up all these music stands and he’d have these signs that he used to carry around “Bernard Purdie Hit Maker” and all kinds — you know like he would just stack them up. So that was his ego showing but you know what, he backed it up with music. He was a really fine drummer. You couldn’t — his ego was worth every cent of it.
I imagine he would sort of butt heads with the producer on occasion, because he knew what was needed?
You know that’s so far back. I don’t ever remember that happened but it’s so far back that I’m not sure that it didn’t happen. Okay?
Is it safe to say that you and your other musicians needed to be musically satisfied because you played just what was required and no more?
Was I musically — well I’m not sure, I might have to rephrase this question. Was I musically satisfied playing what I was playing. Is that better?
Sure.

The answer to that is no. Because at that time in my career I was really studying hard and practicing working on my technique, working on ideas and getting flexible on the guitar and you’d be relegated to playing chics on one and the upbeat of three or something. It was so far away from what I was practicing. But I wasn’t looking for musical satisfaction, I was — no I was looking for musical satisfaction for those songs. I needed those songs, any song that I participated in needed to be played really well. And if I played it well then that’s my satisfaction. It wasn’t to inject something I had been practicing at home on somebody’s record.

That’s a terrific answer. I understand what you’re saying. And when you say you were practicing at that time, what did a practice session normally include for you? Did you focus on one song at a time or learning new chords?

I focused on technique. I used to read out of clarinet technique books and violin technique books. The clarinet is right in the center range on the guitar, it’s really, you can easily incorporate the guitar literature with clarinet literature. And so I would be working on technique. I would be working to get the cleanest technique that I could get, you know if I played a note I wanted the note to come out. I didn’t want like some kind of thud in the background between — in a passage. You know? And I worked on that. I didn’t work © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

on songs, no. I didn’t work on songs. But when I first started playing I worked at — I got a job at the Playboy Club. It came through another guitar player who was leaving and it was a trio job, it was guitar, bass, and piano. The piano player was Monty Alexander and the bass player was Bob Cranshaw. And the guitar player was me. I thought I knew something about the guitar from doing all that studying and playing. But when I got in that jazz situation, those two guys used to beat me up physically — musically — every night, because they were such proficient musicians. They were just off the — I couldn’t figure — I used to go home at night and figure out where they knocked me out in every tune that they knocked me out and there was a regularity there. So as for learning tunes I learned those kind of tunes through them. And I learned — I didn’t learn all the different — I learned different directions to take with harmonies and changes. And that improved — I started to be able to incorporate some of the studies that I did from clarinet and violin just because I had the technique to manipulate between changes. So it was really on-the- job training but heavy on-the-job training by good trainers. That’s how I began.
If they called a tune one night let’s say “What a Difference a Day Makes” and you didn’t know it, so you went home to learn it, first of all how did you access that tune? Did you have fake books?

Okay let me — I have fairly decent ears so when we’re on a session and somebody plays something I can anticipate where the bass line is going. It’s very important for me, the bass line is the key to the thing. And so you hear the harmony on the top, you hear the bass line on the bottom, you almost know where the next change is going to go. So I can anticipate where it’s going to go and I’m ready for it. But Bob and Monty, every once in a while would change the direction and I’d be playing where I think it would go and they’d be playing where they wanted to go. So that’s the kind of studying I had to go home — I didn’t have to learn those tunes. And I knew tons of tunes because I used to play jobs with another guitar player and his wife who was a singer, and you know singers sing fifty tunes a night and so your repertoire builds on the past.
Yes and you often learn them in different keys depending on if it’s a guy or a girl.
Yeah. Right. Yeah.

I had an incident once and it always sticks in my mind, playing in a rock band, but the guitar player was just — played the most beautiful chords and he played something one night and I asked him what it was, what chord is that, because I play piano also. And he held up his hand, he said, “It’s this.” And I said, “Well that doesn’t really help me, can you tell me what the notes are?” And he really couldn’t. He would have to like laboriously look at each string and figure oh okay. But I don’t really have a question here except that guitar seems to be an instrument that you can play a lot of hip chords and so forth and maybe not know exactly what they are? Is that a fair statement? © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

Not to me, no. It’s not really fair. Because if a piano player plays a chord I can hear all the notes in the chord. And there are certain notes when you play a chord, they’re volatile, they want to move in one direction or another, so you’re kind of ready, you can anticipate where they’re going to go. If you’re wrong, you have to make a minor adjustment to fix it. And it’s not a big deal. Or on a guitar from playing a three note chord and I hear that one of these notes is not the same thing I just stop that note from ringing and it’s over. And the time is — it’s such a short amount of time most people wouldn’t even hear — you know I could stop it in the middle of striking with my right hand so I know what to do in those situations. My ear is pretty good so I hear when a piano player plays something I immediately know.
Would you say you have relative pitch?
Yeah. Relative is good. Yeah. It’s not perfect.
Okay. But it’s pretty close.
It’s close, yeah.
Yeah. Just a little bit more about this Playboy Club gig, did you get people coming up and asking for requests and sort of play them on the spot or did you pretty much get left alone?

No we got — okay so the Playboy was with Monty and Bob, there were hardly requests. Because these guys are monster musicians. You want to hear the guy play, you don’t want to pigeon hole him into one little song that your daughter likes or something like that. Yeah. I don’t remember requests coming in. But let me tell you what happened at this Playboy Club. After about maybe eight months or so Bob — I’m sorry Monty got a call for a job at Jilly’s and that was a nightclub in Manhattan that Sinatra used to hang out in and it was a noteworthy club to be in. So Monty left and the group changed. We brought in Larry Willis on piano, Earl May on drums, and the drummer at that time was Dick Berk.
Earl May played the bass?

Yeah. On that job he played electric bass, left handed electric bass. And so Dick Berk was with us and then after a while Dick left and we got Al Foster came in on drums. This group was dynamite. It was too strong for that club, and I’ll tell you what I mean. It was the first exposure to music that anybody walking in the club was exposed to this group. This group was so powerful that they did not want to go to any of the other rooms. They had showrooms, they had a dinner room, they had two rooms upstairs that had shows. And they had a dining room that had a trio. The group was so strong that people would just stay here. And it was worth it, it was just fun. And when we got to work over there we would be bashing from the first note to the end of the job. It was just fun. Nobody © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
wanted to stop playing. It was just, it was the epitome of having a good time playing music. It was just a monster.
Did the management notice that you were keeping people in this one spot and like you’re too good?

They never said you’re too good to us, but they, I’m sure they noticed that people, there was a stairway that they had to walk up to get to the elevators and the stairway was always crowded with people just stopping and listening. And then after, after they’d go, some of them would go to the shows, come down and sit at the piano bar that we were in. It worked out good for everybody.
And how many nights a week did you do this?

Five nights a week. Yeah. But this was during the time when I was working in the studios in the daytime like Monday through Friday, and the Playboy Club Tuesday through Saturday. So any money that I made I did not have a chance to spend it because I was working. Sometimes I’d have the guitar in my hand 12 hours, 16 hours a day, with the studio work and the stuff at night. I had no chance to spend it. It was a chance to bankroll some money at an early part in my career. It was really helpful.
And were you married at the time?
No.
Okay. When you met your future wife, did you tell her my profession is a musician?

No. I mean she knew it because she was friends with I mentioned a guitar player and a singer that I used to work with at the beginning. She was friends with them. She was babysitting for their child and that’s how we started — we met, and she couldn’t help herself, she fell in love and that’s it. But I did not say that I’m a musician so we better watch out. I never felt that we better watch out. I felt comfortable.
I like that. You felt comfortable. And I doubt that then there was a particular time when you had this realization like well I’m making a living playing the guitar.

Yeah, there’s a lot — we were in positions sometimes where I wasn’t sure how much work was coming in or I could see the work coming to an end in a couple of weeks and would something fill in, and it always did fill in. So there was never that un-ease about not being able to make a living.
Did you ever have to have quote — well you had a day gig in the studio, but did you ever have a non-music job along the way?

Yeah but it happened much later. It happened after Dizzy. When I came off the road with Dizzy I got very busy in town. I started working with a lot of singers. I have — I think of myself as an accompanist and singers need to have somebody that knows how to accompany them. They don’t need to have somebody drag them along playing chords behind them. And I have like an understanding of lyrics and when I play, if I’m playing © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

the melody of a song somewhere I’m not just playing the melody, I’m playing the lyric. It’s very important. And singers seem to realize that when I’m working with them. So I began, I started working with a lot of singers in town and after a while they started dying, I mean physically dying. They were Sylvia Syms, Johnny Hartman, Sammy Davis, Susannah McCorkle, you know I mean they were passing away. And I said how am I — I’m never going to be able to fill that spot. The music was starting to change then also. Good singers were getting less and less. It’s almost like today, I mean when I was busy you could name twenty singers. Now you might stop at four you know, it’s just a whole different — it’s a different ballgame. So the singers started dying and I said I will not be able to replace what I have. And I decided to go into the school system and I have a very strong knowledge of mathematics. It comes from my engineering high school days. I went to one of the top schools in New York State so, and it was the kind of school that you had to test to get in, so the requirements were not just ordinary. It wasn’t a local school, students from all over the city would be going to this school that you had to test for. My math background was just tremendous. So I started working in the school system and they found out about my math background. And at that time there was a shortage of teachers so they would make practically anybody, even if they didn’t finish their math careers, they were in the classroom. And I was there to assist them in the classroom. It was just a wonderful time in my life. I found a niche that — I went that direction because here’s what I said to myself — if I get a job that’s going to ask me to travel I’m going, I’m not staying. But it didn’t work out that way. I felt such a connection with the work in high school, I got such a connection with the kids, such a connection with the math, such a connection with the teachers that it was like not even work again it was just fun again. So I had fun, and then I started subbing at the theaters, so during the day over there, working in the theaters a couple of nights a week, and it just kept on — yes I did have a day job, but it was something that I loved. It was really fun.
I just think that’s great. You found another job you loved and had music, you loved that, so you became Mr. Gafa in the school system.
Yeah, no, they used to call me “Mr. Al.”
Oh Mr. Al, okay.
That was okay with me.
I like that.

And let me tell you, one day I came home and, you know, they’re not always great days, and something must have happened at school because I came home and complained. And my wife says, “What do you expect to have fun every day?” I said, “Yeah, okay, this is what I do.” © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

I was fascinated by, you’re talking about accompaniment, because one of my questions I had here was if you accompany somewhat differently playing behind an instrumentalist, Dizzy Gillespie or Sonny Stitt, as you do a vocalist? You started, I think you may have answered it but what would be the difference?

Well when you’re playing with guys like Dizzy they’re constantly changing directions. It’s just — when you’re working with singers you know they don’t change directions too much. They’re pretty much melody singers or they’ll scat a chorus or something like that but they don’t really divert from, they don’t divert from the tune too much. But guys like Dizzy, you know, every note has got the possibility of going somewhere else so it’s — what happens when you play with guys like that you have to play less and less because it gives you more flexibility. As soon as you hear them changing then you’ve got to change the voicing of the chord or a note, one note in the chord or something like that. And so with singers it’s straight ahead and with jazz players you’re on the edge all the time.
Did you replace Mike Longo in his group?

Mike was in the piano — was playing piano when I joined the group so we had a quintet at the beginning. And Mike left after about a year so I didn’t really replace him. But when he left — Mike was the most difficult piano player that I ever worked with. And I can tell you musically why — because he played a lot of chords. He played chords no matter what I played he was playing what he wanted to play in the way of a chord. And there would be these constant conflicts where I’d sit on a note and he would play a note a half a step away from that note and it’s just like somebody’s scratching chalk on a blackboard for me, it just used to drive me up the wall. So he was the only piano player in my life that I really had trouble working with. And when he left we — Dizzy took his salary and split it up and the group opened up harmonically for me, it opened up harmonically for Dizzy. There was — nothing was locked in anymore. And you know I did another four years with Dizzy without a piano.
That’s really so interesting. Did you find yourself, when it was piano and guitar, did you opt at times to just like lay out?

Yeah. Yeah. No I don’t think I ever had to lay out but I had to really be aware of what he was playing. I still was playing with the soloist. The soloist at the time would be Dizzy. And so that was my focus. Every once in a while I’d hear Mike play something and if I think I needed to go get it, I got it. But I never opted out of playing just because Mike was playing, no.
When he — when the solo focus would go to the piano did you play differently?

Yeah. I played according to his solo. Whatever he was doing, he’s the — you know when you’re taking the solo, that’s the word solo, and the rest should be an accompany, in the background yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
When the tables turned and it was a guitar solo —
No.
Getting down in the weeds here.
You don’t even have to finish the question. The answer was no.
Okay. We’ll let our listeners try to figure that little sequence out.
Okay.

I wanted to read something briefly that — I was able to do an interview with Mike and he said this about Dizzy. He was talking about spirituality and the energy in the music, and Mike said about Dizzy, “Energy was pretty much a metaphysical thing that causes the music to have a divine quality to it and Dizzy was aware of the divinity. Dizzy was a celestial being and I saw that. He was the most amazing human being I ever met in my life.” How did you feel about Dizzy?

Well I thought he was a genius. I mean when he played, yeah, he was definitely something not of this earth. He was in another planet when he was doing these things. He played, he was innovative and he was quick and humorous, and if he wanted me to play a chord he would play it in his solo. And if I’m listening I’m hearing it easy. It makes it easy for me. And he heard everything I played. I don’t know how he did that but I’ll give you an example. One night I changed a chord in an original composition, I changed one note in the chord for like a bar, maybe two bars. At the end of the set he said, “Do you want to change the chord?” I said (I’ll be very frank with you) — you know what? I didn’t know he was listening that close but he was. And I said, “No, I don’t want to change the chord, I just wanted to try it out and see what it” — I never did that again, and you know, so he heard everything, he played everything, and he loved to play. He loved to play. And at sound checks in the afternoon before opening up we’d wind up starting a tune and then pretty soon we’re playing and we’re playing a couple of tunes and — because he loved to play. And he was very free with his knowledge, and it was a really astounding five years.

There’s a very humorous story in Bill Crow’s book of Jazz Anecdotes about Dizzy doing a Latin number and the bass player was just supposed to play one note on a particular beat and he lost it and etcetera, it’s a fairly long story, but I wondered if playing Dizzy’s Latin repertoire was something new for you and was it an adjustment?

It was not new and let me tell you we were playing a bunch of my tunes also. So yeah, there was no — you know Dizzy had arrangements on let’s say like “One Note Samba.” He had his arrangement of “One Note Samba.” I didn’t play my arrangement of “One Note Samba,” we played his arrangement. So everything was, it was not new and you tried to be as creative as you can every night. You know you can’t always do that but you © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
try. So no, it was not new, it was, not old hat but it used to change every night. The solos would change every night.
How was he different from, as a leader, from let’s say Carmen McRae?

Oh I knew you were going to bring this up, because this is a really — we’re talking about the sound checks in the afternoon of a new job. Any time — not any time, every time I went on a new job with Carmen she would get into an argument with the club owner or the manager on the afternoon during the sound check, about something. Maybe the lights in the dressing room were not bright, maybe the dressing room needed to be dusted or the rug needed to be vacuumed or this or this. We would start every job with tension. But once she hit the stand and started singing we were in a different atmosphere, it was over. There was none of that came — ever came to the forefront in her performances. And so when I left Carmen I got the call for Dizzy. And I’m saying to myself is this going to be more of the same? And it was absolutely 180 degrees in the opposite direction. It was beautiful. So it was fine. And I need to tell you this first job that I worked with Dizzy, this is with the quintet. It was some joint in Cleveland or something like that I think. And at the end of the first set, and I had never seen his music before, he just called me and we went out. We got on the airplane and so the music is in front and I played it. So before the second set I said to him, I said, “Do you want me to change anything that I’m doing here to help out here?” He said, “If I played the guitar I would play it like you do.” So that’s like, okay, that’s a big relief off me, I don’t have to be tiptoeing around anything. And he was just that kind of — he was inspirational, that’s really inspiring for a musician — go ahead and play, you play whatever you like you know. It works.
That’s a terrific compliment. “If I played the guitar I’d play like you.”
Well I don’t think — maybe he meant — maybe that has some other connotations.
Okay. Did he talk about his Bahái faith much?

Not — he was never preaching to us, but we were always aware that he was a Bahái, yes. And one time we went to Israel and we went to Haifa and he thought he was in heaven over there, because that’s I think the center of where Bahái came from. But he never tried to inject Bahái-ism upon us. And he toed the mark pretty much to their religion, about drugs and drinking and stuff like that.

Mike Longo had mentioned some racial tension when he was with the group, I think the times, the late 60s and early 70s from a social standpoint there was some things that crept into the music business, but I wondered if you ever experienced, because it was a mixed group, and any issues?
Never any issues with the group. Absolutely no issues at all. He was around when my first daughter was born and he was, and so there were no racial issues in that group. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
Every once in a while something would come out but it would be from a foreign entity, not the group.
Glad to hear that. And what did your kids — you have one kid? One child?
Two daughters, yeah.
So do I.
Okay.
Do you — what did they think of your profession?

Now they absolutely love it you know. And they were always aware that I was a guitar player. My youngest daughter had wanted to become a singer. She was a fairly decent singer. How do you — how do you compose? And do you compose on purpose, like I think I’ll write a song today?

No. Okay, there are two ways to compose that I know. One was what you just mentioned. Doc Pomus and Morty Shuman used to spend six and eight hours a day composing. And I didn’t. I would find stuff while I’m practicing or playing and then I’d start to develop it. And I’d develop it into, it would just naturally develop into a tune. So my composing thing comes from practicing and having the guitar in my hands. And the reason I started composing so much is that when I joined the group we were playing a lot of Mike’s tunes and we would play them over and over and over, and I was bored playing the same tunes over and over, so I started writing. And what I started writing fit the group. When I’m in a group situation for a long time I can write for the strengths of the group, it’s very easy, just ‘cause I’m thinking about that group 24 hours a day. And then you think about well maybe this might work and then you develop it and it does work. All right? So I started writing a little more when I was with Dizzy. That was not the first — that was not my first experience with writing, I used to do a lot of these demo dates, I used to do a lot of demo dates for a publishing company, it was called Screen Gems/Columbia Music. And one of the producers said, “Duane Eddy is looking for material for an album.” So I said to myself I could probably write something for that guy, he’s like a hack guitar player. I could write that. So I didn’t really say that, but I thought I could write something simple for this guy to play, and I did. My first composition that I ever presented to anybody was recorded by Duane Eddy. And it was called “Laughing Guitar.” That was not my title, somebody wrote lyrics to it and it got recorded. And then when I was at the Playboy Club with Kai Winding I wrote another thing called “Dirty Dog” and Kai Winding played it. So my stuff has been recorded before Dizzy. Dizzy was just easier to write with Dizzy because we were working 200 days a year and I’m looking to always play some new stuff you know.

You can’t buy a pack of cigarettes, even if you smoked you can’t buy a pack of cigarettes.
Yeah the checks get smaller and the prices are going up.
Yeah. Yeah. Well that’s right, that hits the nail right on the head. Yes — I’m sorry — yes I still get royalty checks for writing and publishing too.

Thank you. You know what? That happens to be my favorite composition. And I got only one bad break on it. Stan Getz wanted to record it. But I would have loved to have him record it because he had all those records with Chick Corea and this tune was — it was the both of them together. And that’s what — I would have loved to have him do that. And it’s been recorded by Al Haig and I think Steve Kuhn and you know, me and Dizzy. It’s my favorite composition. And it was created exactly what you said before. I tune my bottom string to a D, which is like a whole tone below the standard tuning. And I always play with it like that. And I’m using the three open strings on the bottom and they’re vibrating constantly on the bottom ‘cause I’m striking them and then I’m changing the voicings on the top. And so this thing just started with like a D major to a D minor to an E major to a G minor, you know it’s just like moving down and it just felt so good to play. And so there’s a continuation of this story. When I finally got it all together, even the bridge has the same bass pattern. The bass pattern is completely the same throughout the tune except for one little vamp. But it’s still the open D and A in the bottom. It’s just — I hate to say it but it’s a really good tune.
